n: Surprisingly, this “burden” is against Jerusalem itself, called “the valley of vision” — the place of revelation, surrounded by valleys. Why are its people up on the rooftops celebrating?

f.g: Jerusalem, where God gave visions — now blind to its danger.
Flat roofs, where people gathered to celebrate or watch.

n: The city is noisy and partying, but its dead did not even die bravely in battle — perhaps they died of famine or were caught fleeing.

f.g: Full of noise and commotion.

n: Jerusalem’s leaders ran away together and were captured without a single arrow being shot. This may recall the army that fled when Babylon broke in (586 BC), or events in Sennacherib’s invasion (701 BC).

f.w: All thy rulers are fled together

f.g: Captured without the bow — without a fight.

n: Isaiah refuses comfort and weeps bitterly for the destruction of his people.

f.g: A tender name for the nation.

n: It is a day of panic, trampling, and confusion sent by the Lord. Walls are broken down, and cries echo off the mountains.

f.g: Confusion, bewilderment.

n: Elam brings its archers and chariots, and Kir uncovers its shields — foreign troops in the Assyrian army.

f.g: A region in Mesopotamia linked with Aram (Amos 9:7).
Took off the leather cover to prepare for battle.

n: Jerusalem’s best valleys fill with enemy chariots, and horsemen take position at the city gates.
Judah’s defenses are stripped away. In that day the people looked to the weapons stored in the “House of the Forest,” a royal armory built by Solomon.

f.g: Removed the protection.

n: They noticed the many cracks in the walls of David’s city and collected water from the lower pool to survive a siege.

f.g: Breaks or gaps in the wall.

n: They counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore some down to use the stones to strengthen the wall. Archaeologists have found such a wall in Jerusalem built over houses from this period.
They built a reservoir between the walls for water — likely connected with Hezekiah’s famous tunnel — but they never looked to the God who made it all and planned it long ago.

f.w: a ditch between the two walls
f.g: A reservoir; compare Hezekiah’s tunnel and pool (2 Kings 20:20).

f.w: ye have not looked unto the maker thereof

n: On that day the Lord called them to weep, mourn, shave their heads, and wear sackcloth — that is, to repent.

f.g: Shaving the head as a sign of mourning.

n: Instead they partied — slaughtering cattle, eating meat, drinking wine, and saying, “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” Paul and the Book of Mormon both warn against this attitude.

f.w: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die

n: The Lord revealed to Isaiah that this sin will not be forgiven until they die. Their refusal to repent seals their fate.

f.g: Atoned for, covered.

n: Now the Lord sends Isaiah to Shebna, the palace administrator — a powerful royal official.

f.g: The steward of the palace — the king’s chief official.

n: Isaiah challenges him: “What right do you have to carve yourself a grand tomb high in the rock here?” Shebna was building a monument to himself while the nation was in danger. An ancient tomb inscription found near Jerusalem may be his.

f.g: Tomb.

f.w: graveth an habitation for himself in a rock
f.g: Carves a resting place in the cliffside.

n: The Lord will grab hold of him and hurl him away.

f.g: Or “grip you firmly.”

n: God will wad him up like a ball and throw him into a wide land, where he will die far from his fancy tomb. His splendid chariots will become a disgrace to his master’s house.

f.g: A vivid image of being thrown away.

n: God will remove Shebna from his office and position.

f.g: Office, post.

n: Then the Lord will call His servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah to replace him.

f.g: “God establishes.”

n: Eliakim will receive Shebna’s official robe, sash, and authority, and will be like a father to Jerusalem and Judah — a caring, faithful leader.

f.g: Sash of office.

f.w: a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem

n: He will carry the key of David’s house on his shoulder: what he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open. Revelation applies this to Christ, who holds all keys; Latter-day Saints also think of priesthood keys.

f.w: the key of the house of David

n: God will fasten him like a peg driven firmly into a solid wall, and he will bring honor to his family.

f.g: A tent peg or wall peg for hanging things.
A firm, secure spot.

n: His whole family will hang on him like pots and cups hung on a peg — relatives seeking favors and positions.

f.g: Descendants and relatives.
Jars.

n: But eventually even that firm peg will give way under the weight, and everything hanging on it will fall. No human leader can carry everything forever — a warning against nepotism and reliance on mortals.

f.w: the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed
f.g: Many think this refers to Eliakim’s family overburdening him; others to Shebna.
